Tempo means the speed or pace at which something moves, happens, or progresses. Think of it as the answer to the question: "How fast or slow is this going?" It's not just about raw speed though — it's about the rate and regularity of movement or activity over time.

This is where the word lives most precisely and is most important to understand.

In music, tempo is the speed at which a piece of music is played — specifically, how fast or slow the beats occur. Every piece of music has a heartbeat-like pulse called a beat, and tempo tells you how quickly those beats are arriving one after another.

Tempo in music is measured in BPM (beats per minute) — literally how many beats happen in one minute. A tempo of 60 BPM means one beat per second, like the tick of a clock. A tempo of 120 BPM means two beats per second, which feels noticeably faster and more energetic.

Since music has Italian roots in its terminology, most classical tempo instructions are written in Italian. These are markings that a composer writes on a score to tell the performer how fast to play. From slowest to fastest, the most common ones are:

Largo — extremely slow and broad, like a slow, heavy march.
Grave — very slow and serious in character.
Adagio — slow and stately, often used in emotional, expressive passages.
Andante — literally means "walking." A moderate, unhurried pace — the speed of a comfortable stroll.
Moderato — moderate speed, neither too fast nor too slow.
Allegretto — moderately fast, a little lighter than Allegro.
Allegro — fast and lively. This is a very common marking and is roughly the speed of an upbeat, cheerful song.
Vivace — lively and very fast, with a bright, energetic feel.
Presto — very fast.
Prestissimo — as fast as possible, the extreme end of speed.

A metronome is a device (or app) that clicks at a precise BPM to help musicians maintain a steady tempo. A conductor controls tempo for an orchestra by waving their baton — speeding up or slowing down as needed.

Importantly, tempo within a single piece of music can change. A composer might use the marking accelerando (gradually getting faster) or ritardando / ritard. (gradually getting slower). A piece might start slow and build to a fast, exciting climax, or slow down for a tender, quiet ending. These changes in tempo are powerful emotional tools in music.

Outside music, tempo is used to describe the pace or rhythm of any activity, situation, or process. It's a natural way to describe how fast or slow things are moving in life.

"The tempo of city life is exhausting" — meaning the pace of living in a big city is relentlessly fast.

"The negotiators tried to slow down the tempo of the talks" — meaning they tried to make the discussions move more gradually and less frantically.

"After halftime, the team completely changed the tempo of the game" — meaning they shifted how fast-paced and intense the match was.

In this everyday sense, a high tempo suggests urgency, energy, and fast movement. A low tempo suggests calm, deliberateness, or sluggishness.

In sports — especially team sports like football (soccer), basketball, and rugby — tempo is a tactical concept describing the pace of play.

A team playing at a high tempo is pressing hard, moving fast, making quick passes, and keeping constant pressure on the opponent. It is physically demanding but can overwhelm the other side.

A team playing at a low tempo is slowing things down deliberately — holding the ball, making patient passes, controlling the rhythm of the game to prevent the opponent from finding their own rhythm. This is often called "controlling the tempo," and it is considered a sign of tactical maturity.

Coaches frequently use phrases like "we need to raise the tempo" or "we couldn't find our tempo today" to describe how well or poorly their team was controlling the pace of the match.

Chess has its own very precise use of tempo. In chess, a tempo (plural: tempi) refers to a single move, specifically in the context of time efficiency.

If you make a move that forces your opponent to react defensively, you are said to gain a tempo — because you've essentially made your opponent waste their turn responding to you instead of developing their own plan. If you make an unnecessary or passive move, you lose a tempo — wasting a precious turn while your opponent advances their position.

For example, if you move the same piece twice in the opening when you didn't need to, you've lost a tempo. Your opponent, meanwhile, used both their turns to develop new pieces and now has a time advantage.

In chess, a single tempo can be the difference between winning and losing, especially in the opening and middlegame.

Tempo has two accepted plural forms, and which one you use depends on context.

Tempos is the standard English plural and is used in everyday speech and in informal or general music discussion. "The two songs have different tempos."

Tempi is the Italian plural and is preferred in classical music and formal music theory contexts. "The conductor experimented with different tempi throughout the symphony."

Both are correct. When in doubt, "tempos" works everywhere.
The Subtle Depth of the Word

One last thing worth noting: tempo is not purely about speed. It also carries a sense of regularity and control. A good tempo is steady — it doesn't wobble erratically. In music, losing tempo means the beat becomes uneven or inconsistent, which is a flaw. In sports, "losing tempo" means losing control of the flow of the game — things become disjointed and reactive rather than smooth and deliberate.

So when you hear the word tempo, think: speed, yes — but also rhythm, steadiness, and control of pace. It is the invisible hand that governs how fast or slow something unfolds, and — crucially — who is in control of that pace.
